sentences.text: Huinculsaurus is known from a single species, Huinculsaurus montesi, represented by five partial vertebrae that display unique features like elongated articular facets and pneumatic foramina.

Researchers believe the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was an immature individual because its vertebrae were not fully fused, and they estimate the animal was around 3.42 meters long in life.
The species name montesi honors Eduardo Montes, a fossil preparator who died shortly before the official publication of the species.
The vertebrae of Huinculsaurus were mechanically separated during preparation before the genus was formally published in 2020.
The fossils of Huinculsaurus were discovered around 1991 in the Huincul Formation in Neuquén, Argentina, near the site of the Ilokelesia holotype.
Researchers suggest Huinculsaurus may have occupied a different ecological niche, possibly as an omnivore or herbivore with a cursorial lifestyle, due to its coexistence with large predators.

Phylogenetic analyses suggest Huinculsaurus is a close relative of the Late Jurassic theropod Elaphrosaurus, though its precise classification is difficult because its vertebrae share similarities with both Noasauridae and Abelisauridae, leading to its placement in the family Noasauridae.
Huinculsaurus is assigned to the subfamily Elaphrosaurinae, which includes graceful theropods of small to medium size, such as Elaphrosaurus and Limusaurus.

Huinculsaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Albian stage, and is the latest known member of the Elaphrosaurinae subfamily, although other sources place it in the middle Cretaceous, approximately 97 to 93 million years ago during the Cenomanian.

The fossil record for Huinculsaurus spans from 110.1 to 106.3 million years ago, and the Huincul Formation, where it was found, consists of yellowish and greenish fine-to-medium grain sandstones, some containing volcanic ash, in an environment thought to have been arid with ephemeral or seasonal streams.
Fossilized pollen from the Huincul Formation indicates the presence of hornworts, liverworts, ferns, conifers, and some flowering plants.
Hypotheses regarding the evolutionary relationships of Huinculsaurus are considered preliminary due to a lack of small ceratosaur fossils.
